questions.question: What problem do embeddings solve that keyword search cannot?
options: Embeddings store each document as a sparse bag-of-words vector, so rare terms get more weight than common ones at query time
Embeddings index every document inside an HNSW graph, so a plain keyword index can never be searched in less than linear time
Embeddings capture semantic meaning, matching 'payment didn't go through' with 'charge was declined' even though they share no words
Embeddings preserve word order inside a chunk, so that 'dog bites man' and 'man bites dog' can finally be told apart
questions.explanation: Keyword search treats words as independent symbols. Embeddings map text to high-dimensional vectors where semantic similarity = geometric proximity. Texts with the same meaning cluster together regardless of word choice.

questions.question: What does cosine similarity measure between two embedding vectors?
options: The straight-line distance between the two points, which shrinks as the vectors' magnitudes get closer together
The raw inner product of the two vectors, a score that grows whenever either vector's magnitude increases
The number of bits that differ once both vectors have been quantized down to a single bit per dimension
The angle between the vectors, indicating how similar their directions are regardless of magnitude
questions.explanation: Cosine similarity = dot(A,B) / (|A|*|B|). It ranges from -1 (opposite) to 1 (identical direction). Two texts with the same meaning will have vectors pointing in nearly the same direction, giving cosine similarity near 1.

questions.question: What is the typical dimensionality of modern text embedding models?
options: 768 to 3072 dimensions, depending on the model
24 to 64 dimensions, one per layer of the HNSW graph
300 dimensions, the fixed size set in the Word2Vec era
100,000 or more dimensions, one per vocabulary token
questions.explanation: Modern embedding models (OpenAI text-embedding-3, BGE, E5) produce vectors with 768 to 3072 dimensions. Higher dimensions capture more nuance but cost more to store and search.

questions.question: Why should you evaluate embedding quality using retrieval benchmarks rather than just inspecting similarity scores?
options: Cosine similarity ignores vector magnitude, so any two texts of differing length are scored as identical by design
Similarity scores are defined only for normalized embeddings, so a model that skips normalization returns no number
Similarity scores are computed after HNSW pruning, so they report the index's recall rather than the quality of the embedding model
Absolute similarity values vary by model; what matters is whether relevant documents outrank irrelevant ones (precision@k, recall)
questions.explanation: A cosine similarity of 0.85 might mean 'very similar' for one model and 'somewhat similar' for another. Retrieval metrics (precision@k, recall) measure what actually matters: does the right document come back?

questions.question: When would you use a local/open-source embedding model instead of an API-based one?
options: When you need Matryoshka truncation, which only open-weight checkpoints expose via a dimensions parameter
When you need data privacy, offline operation, lower cost at scale, or domain-specific fine-tuning
When the corpus passes a million vectors, since hosted APIs cannot return more than the top-k nearest results
When retrieval quality is the priority, because hosted models always score below open-weight ones on MTEB
questions.explanation: API embeddings (OpenAI, Cohere) are easy but send your data externally. Local models (BGE, E5, Nomic) keep data private, eliminate per-call costs at scale, and can be fine-tuned on domain-specific data.
